name: One-state solution
summary: The one-state solution proposes ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict with a single democratic state in the whole of former Mandatory Palestine, instead of partition into two states. Its advocates hold that partition has failed and that Israel already rules the whole land as one unequal state; they call for equal citizenship for everyone living there, the return of Palestinian refugees, the end of Jewish legal privilege and of Zionist colonization, and a non-sectarian state. They differ on whether the state should be unitary, recognising individuals, or binational, recognising two national communities.
scope: The one-state solution as the defining scholarship describes it: Farsakh's edited volume Rethinking Statehood in Palestine (s1: her introduction and chapter 7, and Mazen Masri's chapter 9 on constitutional frameworks) traces it from Brit Shalom and Ihud's binationalism and the PLO's 1970 democratic-state programme to its revival since 1999, and presents today's debate as one between a unitary democratic state and a binational state. The profile follows that contemporary proposal, read in the texts Farsakh and her contributors name: Tilley's essay The One-State Solution (s2), the 2007 One State Declaration (s3), the One Democratic State Campaign programme (s4, s5), Judt's case for a binational state (s6), and the Popular Movement for One Democratic State's points (s8). Where the unitary and binational strands disagree the answer is a split. Excluded: Israeli right-wing annexation plans that keep a Jewish state, Islamist or Iranian calls for a Palestinian state replacing Israel, Gaddafi's Isratin plan, and the 'one-state reality' described by observers, which are other subjects.

notes: First pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-10); no statement-pass library existed, so the source library was built here. Scope follows Farsakh's volume (s1), which defines today's one-state debate as one between a unitary democratic state and a binational state; where the two strands disagree (territorial autonomy, power sharing, collective rights) the answer is a split or low. The ODSC programme (s4, s5) is used as the campaign's own statement of what the one democratic state is, and mostly alongside the Declaration or the scholarship. Themes searched: government (democracy, constitution, entrenched rights, electoral system, parliamentary system, separation of powers, federalism and consociationalism), liberty and rights (equal citizenship, non-discrimination, individual versus collective rights), society and culture (religion and the state, languages, cultural autonomy, ethnicity and nationhood, settler colonialism, redress and transitional justice), world (self-determination, partition, refugees and return, immigration, international law, the region), and economy (redistribution, the economic dimension of decolonization). Most economic, ecological, technological, gender and criminal-justice questions are not addressed by the one-state sources, and the means of struggle (BDS, armed struggle) belong to allied movements rather than to the proposal as its sources define it, so those statements are null. Not reached: Edward Said's 1999 New York Times Magazine essay 'The One-State Solution' (nytimes.com and the one-state.org copy refused scripted access), the CounterPunch copy of the One State Declaration and Barghouti's ZNetwork essay (refused). Ali Abunimah's One Country has no open copy. Read but not cited: Barghouti's Red Pepper essay (it does not name the proposal in a way the source check can tie), the Fatah 1970 pamphlet (scanned columns; Farsakh's account of it is used instead), Hermann's article on the bi-national idea, the Stuttgart conference declaration and Falk's message on the Houston Declaration (conference statements of solidarity groups).
